commented_code_element: a syntactic unit of source code that has been rendered inactive by enclosing it in comment syntax, producing no observable execution behavior while remaining visible in the source text.
comment_syntax_container: the comment delimiters and surrounding text that physically bind the disabled code element, making its source legible but its semantics inert.
dead_execution_state: the condition of a code element whose source text exists but whose semantics are excluded from runtime interpretation.
rationale_annotation: an explanatory comment accompanying commented-out code that documents the reason for its disablement, often speculative or stale.
temporal_marker: metadata within or adjacent to commented code that indicates when it was disabled, such as a date, version number, or commit reference.
resurrection_intent: an expressed or implied intention within commented code to re-enable it in the future, typically indicated by TODO, FIXME, or similar markers.
version_control_anchor: the commit, branch, or revision at which the code element was disabled, serving as the authoritative record of its prior active state.
observer_agent: a developer or automated system that encounters commented-out code during maintenance, reading, or modification activities.
confusion_signal: the observable cognitive overhead or maintenance uncertainty experienced by an observer when encountering commented-out code without clear justification.
maintenance_burden: the increased cost of change—measured in time, risk, or error likelihood—imposed by commented-out code on future development activities.
code_smell: a surface indicator in source code that suggests a potential deeper problem in design or implementation, of which commented-out code is one instance.
substitution_pair: an active code element that replaces or is intended to replace a commented-out element, establishing a functional successor relationship.

A data_clump is a group of two or more variables that appear together as a repeated pattern across three or more distinct call sites or declarations, indicating a missing cohesive abstraction.
A clump instance is a concrete occurrence where a specific set of variable names or types travel together as a bound unit across multiple locations.
A clump signature is the canonical ordered set of variable names and types that define a recurring data group, used to match equivalent clumps across sites.
A clump site is a distinct lexical location where the clump variables appear together, such as a function signature, method call, or field declaration.
Parameter clump is a data_clump that manifests as a group of method or function parameters that repeat together across multiple call sites.
State clump is a data_clump that manifests as a group of instance or class fields that are always initialized or mutated together.
Contextual clump is a data_clump where the same primitive variables appear together but only within a specific subsystem or feature boundary.
Missing abstraction is the root cause condition where no class, struct, or record type encapsulates a recurring variable group, forcing clients to manage the group manually.
Clump threshold is the minimum repetition count (typically three or more distinct sites) required before a variable group qualifies as a detected data_clump smell.
Clump extraction is the refactoring operation that introduces a new type to represent the data group and replaces repeated variable declarations with instances of the new type.
the new parameter or field of candidate_abstraction type that replaces the entire clump_instance at a call site.
a candidate class or record type whose fields would mirror the clump_instance members, enabling replacement of the raw variables with a typed object.

an integer metric: the number of distinct call sites or scopes where the same variable set appears together.
an integer metric: the minimum cooccurrence_count that qualifies a variable set as a clump_instance (commonly two or more).

a clump_instance whose co-occurred variables are instance fields of one or more classes.

a clump_instance whose co-occurred variables are formal parameters of one or more method signatures.
a code location where the clump_instance appears, serving as a refactoring entry point.

long_parameter_list: a method or function whose parameter signature exceeds a comfortable cognitive threshold, typically citing more than three or four distinct arguments, making the interface awkward to call and maintain
caller_signature_clone: a pattern where multiple call sites pass the same subset of parameters to a method, signaling that those parameters form a logical unit awaiting formalization as an object
signature_change_ripple: the cascade of modifications required across all call sites when a long parameter list is altered, representing the brittleness cost of the current design
parameter_cognitive_load: the mental effort required to recall the order, type, and purpose of each argument at every call site, which degrades rapidly as parameter count increases

data_clump_association: the kinship between long_parameter_list and data_clump, where the same fields appear together repeatedly across methods and constructors, both pointing toward a missing abstraction

extract_parameter_grouping_method: splitting a long-parameter method into smaller methods that each receive a coherent subset of parameters, addressing the long method smell alongside the long parameter list

introduce_parameter_object_refactoring: a transformation that replaces a long parameter list with a single parameter object class, grouping related data and enabling method reuse and invariant enforcement
cross_parameter_invariant: a constraint or business rule that logically spans two or more separate parameters but cannot be enforced because the parameters lack a shared container object
long_method_cooccurrence: the empirical pattern that methods with long parameter lists frequently also suffer from excessive length and complexity, as both stem from insufficient decomposition
preserve_whole_object_refactoring: a technique that passes the source object itself rather than extracting and passing individual attributes, reducing parameter count by restoring object cohesion

primitive_parameter_bundle: a set of primitive values that travel together through multiple method signatures, frequently indicating a missing abstraction that could be encapsulated into a coherent parameter object

primitive_obsession_association: the tendency to pass multiple primitives instead of a richer object, feeding the long_parameter_list problem and suggesting that introducing a parameter object also addresses primitive obsession

replace_parameter_with_method_call: a refactoring that eliminates a parameter by having the method obtain the value itself, applicable when the callee can compute the argument from existing parameters or object state
test_fixture_burden: the difficulty of constructing meaningful test cases when a method requires many parameters, often leading to tests that omit or default critical arguments

parameter_count_threshold: the line of demarcation beyond which a parameter list is deemed excessive, commonly cited as three to four parameters in literature, though context and team conventions may shift this boundary
